paragraphs.text: In the present work we have undertaken to write a defence of the prophet David. He does not need this service, since he shone with such great merits and flourished in virtues. But many people read the course of his deeds without looking into the force of the Scriptures or the hidden meaning of their mysteries, and they wonder how so great a prophet failed to avoid the taint first of adultery and then of murder. That is why we have made it our task to go back over the story itself.

…which seems to have lain open to sin. For in the Second Book of Samuel we read that David, walking about in his royal house, looked out and saw a woman bathing. Her name was Bathsheba, and she was exceptionally beautiful, lovely in grace and countenance, and of quite outstanding looks. Softened by these allurements, he conceived the desire to possess her. Now the woman was married, and her husband's name was Uriah. By the king's orders a scheme was set up for his death. For although his being alive was thought to be no hindrance to the king's desire, it was thought to stand very much in the way of keeping the adultery decently hidden.

So, to begin with the plainer points: do not pass judgment on one whom God has justified. "It is a very small thing to me," says Paul, "that I should be judged by you or by any human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself." He was still in the body, still liable to temptation, yet he did not judge himself, because the spiritual man is judged by no one but God alone. Then he added: "It is the Lord who judges me. Therefore do not judge anything before the time." But David has already fulfilled his time. He has earned grace and been justified by Christ, since the Lord himself rejoiced to be called the son of David, and those who confessed him in this way received light. Why do you call a man of God away from his reward to face judgment? The Lord has already judged him. Of him the Lord said to Solomon: "If you walk before me as David your father walked, in holiness of heart and in righteousness, so as to do according to all that I commanded him." Does this man, then, deserve judgment or reward, when he did according to all the heavenly commands, walking in holiness and righteousness of heart? Where the sins and vices of others lie hidden, there David received God's testimony to his virtue and glory. And we sit idly disputing about the sin of the man whose merit and favour caused the sins of others to be lightened [?]! For when Solomon had offended by not keeping the commandments of the Lord, and God had resolved to split his kingdom into many parts, he said to him: "Yet I will not do these things in your days, for the sake of David your father. I will take it from the hand of your son. Yet I will not take away the whole kingdom; I will give one sceptre for the sake of David my servant." Since the Lord justifies him, then, who is it who passes judgment on so great a man? "What God has cleansed," it says, "you must not call common."

Still, leaving the heavenly judgment intact, so that you too may honour so great a prophet, look into his acts and character. Do you not marvel at this man? For most of his life you would judge him equal to the angels. From boyhood he lived among riches, honours and power, and was placed in many temptations. Yet he gave way to error only once, and it was an error by which even the angels of heaven, as Scripture records, were cast down from their grace and power. Admittedly, another error of his is also recorded: he had the people counted.

How many faults each of us commits every hour! And yet ordinary people do not think their sins need confessing. That king, so great and powerful, did not let the awareness of his offence stay with him for even a brief moment. By prompt confession and immense grief he rendered his sin up to the Lord. Find me now, if you easily can, a man of honour and wealth who would not take it badly if he were accused of some fault. Yet David, illustrious with royal power and approved by so many divine oracles, was rebuked by a private man for having sinned grievously, and he did not roar with indignation. Instead he confessed and groaned with grief for his fault. The grief of his inmost feeling then moved the Lord, so that Nathan said: "Since you have repented, the Lord has also put away your sin." The speed of the pardon therefore showed that the king's repentance was deep, deep enough to carry away the offence of so great an error.

When other men are rebuked by priests, they make their sin worse by trying to deny or defend it, and their fall becomes greater at the very point where correction is hoped for. But the saints of the Lord long to complete the holy contest and to run the course of salvation. If, being human, they happen to fall somewhere, more through the frailty of nature than through a lust for sinning, they rise up keener to run, spurred on by shame, and make up for it with greater contests. So their fall is reckoned not only to have caused no hindrance but even to have piled up incentives to greater speed. When some runners happen to fall, the race is not called off. Nor are the wrestlers' bouts; the contests go on unharmed. In fact many have won with greater credit after one or two falls. How much more, then, should those who have entered the contest of piety not be judged by the offence of a single slip! For blessed is the one who can recover himself after a fall, since to rise again even after death is the gift of the blessed.

We can also see that sin is profitable in another way, and that offences crept up on the saints by the Lord's providence. They are set before us to imitate, and so care was taken that they too should sometimes fall. If they had finished their course untouched by vice amid all the slippery places of this world, they would have given us, who are weaker, reason to think that they were of some higher and divine nature, unable to admit sin or have any share in guilt. That opinion would certainly have deterred us, who have no part in such a nature, from attempting an impossible imitation. So God's grace passed them by for a little while, so that their life might become a discipline for us to imitate, and so that we might learn from their acts how to repent as well as how to be innocent. So when I read of their falls, I recognize that they shared our weakness too; and when I believe that they shared it, I take it that they are to be imitated.

The apostle Paul also reminds us that the Lord our God took precautions. Even in the saints, human feeling might become puffed up through the sublimity of revelations or a continuing run of successful works. They might then credit to themselves and attribute to their own virtue what had been granted them by God's working. So, to keep them from falling into so great a judgment and dropping into the pit of faithlessness, the Lord allowed fault to creep in upon them, so that they too might notice that they need divine help and recognize that they must seek the guide of their salvation. Indeed, Paul testifies that weakness profited him. When he begged that the goad in his flesh be taken from him, the Lord said to him: "My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness." And rightly he boasts of his weaknesses, for he knew that many, even among the saints, had fallen beyond remedy through an abundance of virtue. How much better, then, to have given room to one or two reproaches than to have brought upon oneself the lasting displeasure of God!

Need I add what we can infer from the ordinary practice of the world? When we have proved many people in one office, we want to test them, as diligent and energetic people, in another task. How many athletes who have excelled in one kind of contest are called to another! What if the Lord your God, once you have given some proof of your virtue, also wants to test you in another kind of virtue? Holy Job was running without stumbling, yet God allowed him to be tested by the death of his children and by sores over his whole body. In this way God proved his virtue in this respect too: whether he would lessen his devotion even when driven by injuries and bitter sufferings. Is it not clear, then, that God also wished to test holy David, noble in faith, outstanding in gentleness, strong of hand, to see how he would cover a fault and amend a fall, so as to teach us how we might cover a sin we have committed?

Perhaps someone thinks it a poor reason that so great a prophet erred for the sake of our correction. Yet for the redemption of all Christ took on our infirmities, and he who knew no sin was made sin for us. Is it thought unworthy and unlikely, then, that David incurred the reproach of one fall to benefit those who came after him? The Lord himself was made a reproach for us, as he says: "But I am a worm and no man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people," and elsewhere: "and the reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me." So he first sent the mystery of the dispensation to come ahead in his own people. The lowly servants bore the sins of their own condition, and so they themselves could not be free of sin. But the Lord took up a burden that was not his own, and so he alone had no share in offences.

In short, the apostle's teaching too has shown us that many things done in earlier times were done as figures. He said that the fathers bitten by serpents in the desert could be healed in no other way than by Moses hanging up a bronze serpent. At the sight of it those deadly bites and harmful infusions of venom were cured. Then he added: "These things happened to them as figures, for our correction." The bronze serpent, as if nailed to a cross, was a figure, because the true one who was to be crucified was being announced to the human race. He would drain away the venom of the serpent, the devil. In figure he was accursed, but in truth he would wipe out the curses of the whole world. Elsewhere too, writing to the Galatians, Paul says that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. He added: "The son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, the son of the free woman through the promise. These things are said by way of allegory." In what follows he clearly explained what "by way of allegory" means. Those two lines of birth, one from the slave woman and the other from the free woman, are two covenants. The first is from Mount Sinai, the mountain on which Moses received the law from the Lord, and it bears children into slavery. The other is from Jerusalem, which is free. She bore children in Isaac, that is, in the freedom of grace and not in the slavery of the letter, for punishment is decreed for slaves, while grace is granted to the free. Did not Jacob take two wives, as a type of the two peoples, and beget different offspring from them? Why do we read that the patriarch Judah sought to lie with his own daughter-in-law after his son's death, which led to the birth of twins? Surely it was so that a figure might go ahead of both testaments of the Lord Jesus, one established as a type of his coming death, the other in the truth of the gospel. The figure showed that two peoples were to be born, and that the later of them, by the sign of the cross, would cut through every hedge and fortification of the earlier people. This is the people that was first by the hand and last by birth. Or else it was because the Lord Jesus himself, born of the tribe of Judah, sent his works ahead before he was born to us of a virgin.

What shall I say of Joseph? His brothers turned on him, stripped him of the garment his father gave him, threw him into a pit, and sold him into slavery. In this he gave a clear sign of the Lord's incarnation. For the Lord, beloved of the Father, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, came among us, and humbled himself even to death on a cross. Bought and sold by his own brothers, he redeemed the human race by the price paid for him. As a type of him, David was chosen as the youngest of his brothers and anointed to the kingdom. Alone, in a grave danger of war, he freed the whole people by single combat and triumphed over ten thousands, so that girls sang with timbrels: "Saul has triumphed over thousands, and David over ten thousands." What do those young girls figure but souls singing the psalm of triumph to Christ? David begot sons, one incestuous and another who sought to kill his father. This was because an incestuous and parricidal people would violate the flesh of its own Author when it was fixed to the gibbet of the cross. Indeed, the title of the third psalm names Absalom, and the psalm prophesies the Lord's passion.

What shall I say of holy Solomon? His later life is not free of grave error, yet the Jewish common people think that he himself came as the Christ. And how many people has the offence of his grave error called back from that mistake! So the greater fault did more good: it kept a man who was not free of human vice from being believed to be more than human. In him, then, there was a wisdom that drew envy and a fault that persuaded, for it proved him a man.

What then prevents us from believing that Bathsheba too was joined to holy David as a figure? She would signify the gathering of the nations, which had not been joined to Christ by any lawful marriage of faith, because it was to enter into his grace by certain back entrances, outside what the law prescribes. In it, naked sincerity of mind and open simplicity, through the justifying mystery of the washing, would win over the mind of the true David, the eternal King, and stir his love. Rightly he came in secret, to deceive the prince of this world, who is like that Uriah, whose name means "my light," and who disguises himself as an angel of light. He came, I say, into this world, and he came in secret. He entered like an adulterer, to claim his lawful right.

We have set out what we consider strong arguments and have shown that the text of this story was a figure. Now let us go back to what came before and examine the error as if stripped of its spiritual garments. David sinned, as kings usually do. But he did penance, wept and groaned, which kings do not usually do. He confessed his guilt, begged for pardon, lay on the ground lamenting his misery, fasted and prayed, and by making his grief public he handed down the testimony of his confession to all ages. What private persons are ashamed to do, the king was not ashamed to confess. Those who are bound by laws dare to deny their sin and scorn to ask for the pardon that he sought, though he was bound by no human laws. That he sinned belongs to our human condition; that he pleaded for mercy belongs to amendment. The fall is common, but the confession is rare. To have fallen into fault, then, is a matter of nature; to have washed it away is a matter of virtue. "Who will boast," it says, "that he has a pure heart?" By the testimony of Scripture, not even an infant one day old is declared clean.

Show me anyone who has never slipped into sin. Samson is described as the strongest of all; he even strangled a lion with his bare hands. If only he could have choked his own love! He set fire to the harvests of the Philistines, yet he himself was set on fire by the little flame of one woman. Jephthah came back victorious over the enemy, but as he brought home the banners of triumph he was conquered by his own oath. He thought that his daughter's devotion in coming out to meet him had to be repaid by killing her. First of all, what need was there to swear so readily and to vow uncertain things as though they were certain, when he did not know how they would turn out? And then, does anyone pay grim oaths to the Lord God, discharging his vows with bloody funerals?

Nor do I think the priests should be passed over in silence, lest I seem to be hiding our own faults. Aaron himself was high priest, and under his leadership, together with Moses, the Hebrew people crossed the Red Sea on foot. Yet when the people asked him to make them gods to worship, he demanded gold and threw it into the fire, and the head of a calf was formed, to which sacrifices were offered. This made it plain that the desire for gold is the raw material of faithlessness, and that sacrileges are commonly born of eager greed. Again, so great a priest fell into an offence together with his sister Miriam. While the two of them were disparaging their brother for having taken a foreign wife, Miriam at once broke out with the contagion of spotted flesh.

In this there was a figure of a plain mystery. That priestly people of the fathers would in later times disparage its brother people, not knowing the sacrament of that Ethiopian woman. If it had known, it would not have censured what agreed with the ancient mystery. So when a Jew says that someone who has come to faith from among the Gentiles is common, and wants to separate him from the law, he has leprosy. He will not be able to escape it unless a spiritual understanding of the law helps him to obtain pardon.
So David too, knowing that he was a man born to fall, asked for pardon and did not despair of the Lord's mercy.

Nor does the parable seem to differ from the mystery. For who is the rich man but our Lord Jesus? As we heard read today, he says of himself that a certain man, being rich, went away into a far country to receive a kingdom and to return. And truly he was rich, in the wealth of his majesty and the fullness of his own divinity. Angels and archangels, virtues and powers and principalities, thrones and dominions, Cherubim and Seraphim served him with tireless obedience. Yet, rich as he was, he left the ninety-nine sheep on the mountains and went looking for the one sheep that had been left behind, exhausted. The prince of this world, needy and poor compared with that rich man, was feeding this sheep on his own food, like a daughter. No wonder she had grown weak, since her sustenance was the food of the world. This sheep had strayed in Adam, lured by the snares of the serpent.

Yet she was not a bad sheep, for she was full of the Word, being the daughter of the rational week and the gift of the holy Creator. Still, for a long time she was fed not on anything precious but on the cheap resources of the poor man. Indeed, it says, "she ate of his bread and drank from his cup and slept in his bosom." The food of the Ethiopians is not good; Babylon, the golden cup that makes the nations drunk, is harmful. Sleep does those who sleep no good; I would rather keep awake. Indeed, "all the foolish of heart were troubled; they slept their sleep and found nothing." So, for hospitality's sake, because he had received a guest and wanted to set a meal before him, he took the poor man's lamb. If he had sacrificed some animal from his own flocks or herds, it could not have benefited us. Unless he had sacrificed what was ours, he would not have redeemed us.

So with a kind of hospitable affection he took the infirmities of our frail nature into his own flesh. To relieve that frailty, or rather to restore it, he offered his flesh to that saving passion, to provide us with the food of eternal life. And Scripture rightly called it a ewe lamb, because it was the offspring of a virgin. Rightly too is this rich man declared worthy of death by the prophet's judgment, for Caiaphas also prophesied, saying: "It is expedient that one man should die for the people." Only the Lord Jesus was chosen as worthy of such a death, a death by which he would take away the sin of the world. It also added, beautifully: "He shall restore the lamb," because he raised up his own flesh and restored that flesh of virginal purity. Nor is it idle that it says: "He shall restore it fourfold." For the resurrection of the dead is fourfold, as the apostle teaches when he says: "It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown an animal body, it rises a spiritual body." He will certainly restore the lamb fourfold in another way as well, in that a man can now say: "If I have taken anything from anyone, I restore it fourfold." Fittingly, too, it added: "because he did not spare"; for Christ did not spare himself, so that he might come to the help of all.

And therefore, to declare the mystery, the Lord Jesus Christ said to his servant David: "Because you did this in secret, I will do this thing before all Israel and in the sight of this sun." At first, not knowing the sacrament, David was moved to indignation, yet his feeling did not go astray. But afterwards he recognized the great mystery, for great is the sacrament of Christ and the Church. He saw the forgiveness of all sins that was to come, and foresaw the radiance of grace through the washing of regeneration and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Then, confident of pardon, he said: "I have sinned against the Lord," so that he too might come into the fellowship of those who would receive forgiveness of their guilt. Do you see how he lamented his own sin? Who, then, would be surprised that it was forgiven him?

Now let us consider his works, by which he was able to cover his sin. Since human frailty cannot be without sin, we must take care that our sins do not outnumber our works of virtue. Saint Paul expressed this with the great force of his wisdom when he said: "The sins of some men are plain to see, going before them to judgment; but in others they follow after." That is, no one is found untouched by fault: a person has good merits, but also vices and sins. So everything of ours is weighed as if in a balance. If our sins outweigh our good deeds, they go before us to judgment. Sins sink down as if into the depths. Those that are plain to see sink down, whether through their weight and bitterness or through their number. "But in others," he says, "they follow after." That is, there are those who have lived soberly but, through the frailty of their condition, have sometimes given way to error. Their good deeds go first, and their evil deeds follow. These are more honourable, but they are still people who have slipped into lighter vices and errors. So sins follow the just and do not go before them, but they go before the unjust. The sins that sink down outweigh the rest, and whatever has been done rightly follows behind, weighed down as if by the prior verdict of the sins that went before. In the same way good deeds are also plain to see, for they shine with the working of virtue and the splendour of merit, and things that are the opposite cannot be hidden. So sins like these are not covered. The love that covers a multitude of sins does not overshadow them, the grace of good works does not cover them, and a multitude of virtues does not hide them. They are exposed, as if naked and uncovered. For among such people there is no one to say: "Protect me under the shadow of your wings." And it is the cross of the Lord that blots out and hides all errors.

Who, then, covered and concealed more than holy David? Elsewhere he says, "And in the shadow of your wings I have hoped, until iniquity passes by," and he loved the Lord so much that by the greatness of his love he covered and hid every sin. The holy apostle Peter wiped out his fall by confessing his love. The Lord asked him a third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?", so that he might confess three times the one he had denied three times, and so hide the fall of his threefold denial under a kind of threefold veil of love. If Peter won pardon because he wept once, how much more David, who washed his bed every night and watered his couch with tears, whose tears were his bread day and night, who ate ashes like bread and mingled his drink with weeping! For if Jesus has mercy on the one who turns and groans, if he looked at Peter and Peter wept, how much more will he have mercy on one who wept for a long time and never withdrew from the Lord's sight? Peter denied and did not weep, because Jesus had not looked at him. He denied a second time and did not weep, because the Lord had not looked at him. He denied a third time, Jesus looked at him, and at once he wept, and wept most bitterly. That is why David, who was always weeping, said, "My eyes are ever toward the Lord"; and because Christ always saw him, he said, "My eyes have run down with streams of water."

But now let us consider his deeds as well. Who would not let the praise of such great virtues overshadow the odium of a single crime? Chosen by God's own judgment, he proved at once that he was not unworthy of so great a verdict. He went out to battle, and while the rest trembled, he alone met the foreigner Goliath, a man made terrifying by his boastful words and his huge bulk, and laid him low with faith and courage together. The bravery of one man became the victory of all. Let us compare, if you like, a private crime with the triumph of all, the death of one man with the life of whole peoples, of the many he freed from death.

Let us come to other things. He suffered plots from the king, who sought to put an end to his life. But when by God's dispensation the king was delivered into his power and lay wholly open to a wound, holy David stopped his companions as they were about to strike. He turned the deadly blow away from the body of a man who would otherwise have perished, saying, "Do not touch the Lord's anointed." More than that, he even avenged his enemy's death, mourned his end with many tears, and for a long time put off taking the kingdom that was due to him, which he knew was due to him by God's own authority. By this alone he taught all men that a kingdom must not be seized beforehand, even if it is owed, but must be waited for until it is conferred in its own time. If only later generations had imitated this man! We would not have endured such bitter wars. You reproach him for killing one man; you do not consider that he taught how lasting peace might be kept for the Roman world. How heavy is the devastation with which we are still paying! With what public funeral, as it were, of the whole world have we atoned for the murder of a king who was attacked! Alas, what harsh punishments! Because of this the barbarian enemy still mocks us, while arms prepared against him are turned against us. So the strength of the state has fallen; so Roman valor, broken by its own upheavals, has grown old, while what was undertaken with a father's devoted care is snatched away by a parricide against the state. David guarded against this so carefully that when he learned that his son Adonijah was usurping the kingdom and gathering assemblies, he chose not the son who was eager to seize it beforehand, but the one who was willing to wait.

The mightiest of kings danced before the ark of the Lord. When his own wife rebuked him for having stripped himself before the eyes of the maidservants, he answered: "Before the Lord I will be stripped still further, and I will be a fool in your eyes, so that the Lord may be honored, who chose me for the kingdom in place of your father." He was teaching that no thought of royal power should be kept where homage is being paid to religion. For it is honorable to act for the sake of religion, even if the act is unbecoming to power.

Look at another memorable thing. A parricidal son had violently seized his father's kingdom. At first his father gave way to his fury and avoided meeting him in battle, so that even in this way the impious son might come to his senses from his madness. He also refused to take part in the battle, and asked those setting out to fight to spare his son. The one who asked them to spare him was sure of victory; and he was no stranger to fatherly love, since he did not think that even an impious son ought to perish. He wept, and with great grief lamented the death of the parricide, saying, "My son Absalom, who will grant me to die for you, my son Absalom?" He thought that the man who had killed him to avenge the wrong done to a father deserved punishment himself.

How patient he was under injury and pain! As [?] he was giving way to the fury of his son Absalom, though he was flanked right and left by strong warriors, a man named Shimei cursed him, calling him bloodstained, a man of blood, and saying that he had been cast out of the kingdom by the just judgment of the Lord. Yet he was not moved even by such insults; his companions were. Then one of his comrades, a man named Abishai, threatened to take off Shimei's head as the price of the insult. But the king turned to Abishai and said, "What have I to do with you, son of Zeruiah? He curses me because the Lord told him to curse." How well he taught the moral lesson that the times of our injuries and dangers are contests of temptation and tests of proving, and are therefore not usually inflicted without God's judgment! The good athlete is trained by insults, trained by labors and dangers, so that he may be worthy to receive the crown of righteousness. So the things thought to be adversities must be borne patiently. Divine Scripture teaches you this elsewhere too, when the righteous man says: "If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?"

And the holy prophet added: "Behold, my son, who came out of my womb, seeks my life. And if a Benjaminite curses me, let him curse, because the Lord has told him to, so that he may see my humiliation; and the Lord will repay me for this cursing." O depth of prudence! O signal patience! O great discovery for swallowing an insult! "Are you troubled, Abishai," he says, "that a stranger curses me, when my own son seeks my life by parricide? The Lord told him to curse me." But the Lord is no curser, and he takes no delight in insults.

See how carefully he guards each point. He does not accuse the Lord as though he were the author of the injury; rather, he praises him because he himself suffers it. We ... [?] to endure lesser things, so that we may obtain pardon for greater sins. See how the insult of words lightened the affliction of parricide! He acquitted the insolent man, whose curses do him more good, since they are rewarded by God's recompense. Who would not reckon such an injury a fair exchange, when God consoles with better things the one whom man has wounded?

Let us consider his other deeds too. He fought against the race of giants when one of them had nearly struck down the king as he was engaged in battle; but the enemy paid for that daring with the death he met.

Having won this triumph over a fierce and defeated nation, he again took on a terrible war in the Valley of the Titans, no less against nature than against the enemy. For he was thirsty while he was engaged in the war, and he had nothing to drink. "Who," he said, "will give me a drink from the cistern that is in Bethlehem by the gate?" Between the cistern and holy David lay the enemy, with the enclosure of the hostile camp in between. Three men cut through the mass of the enemy, drew water from the cistern in Bethlehem, and brought it to the king to drink. But the king would not drink it and poured it out to the Lord. It was fitting for so great a gift that what had been the sign of vigorous courage should become a sacrifice of devotion. And he spoke words worthy of the prophetic spirit: "Far be it from me to do this, lest I drink the blood of men who went at the risk of their lives." So he conquered nature, refusing to drink though he was thirsty, and offered himself as an example by which the whole army might learn to endure thirst. He also trained his subjects in the duty of courage, so that soldiers would willingly obey the king's command even through dangers. By refusing to drink he showed that he had given the command to test his soldiers, not because he was overcome by the need of thirst. He showed too that he had taken care that no king should seek the enjoyment of a drink through the dangers of others. Finally, he showed that he had prayed to be spared a wound to his devout conscience, since water sought at the cost of so many men's blood could have no sweetness to the taste, bound up as it was with the horror of the death they had faced.

But if you wish to look more deeply and see into the mystery, David was not thirsting for water from the cistern in Bethlehem. Rather, he foresaw in the spirit Christ, who would be born of the Virgin. So he wished to drink not river water but the drink of spiritual grace. That is, he thirsted not for the element of water but for the blood of Christ. That is why he did not drink the water offered to him but poured it out to the Lord. He was signifying that he thirsted for the sacrifice of Christ, not for a stream of nature: for that sacrifice in which there would be forgiveness of sins, for that eternal fountain which would not be sought at the risk of others but would drive away the dangers of others.

After so many and such wonderful works, then, do we not believe that the blood of one man was covered? The voice of righteous Abel's blood rightly cried out to the Lord, because wicked Cain was covered by no good works, because he had murdered his own kin, because he did not confess his crime but denied it. David, on the other hand, had indeed killed a man who was not at all guilty. But he killed not from any zeal for cruelty, but to cover his shame and hide the disgrace of his lust. I do not dare to say that he was crushed by the force of crime, for a man who knew how to raise himself from that ruin of sin was not crushed. But I do say that he was bent by the force of temptation. For he had said earlier, "Prove me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart"; and elsewhere, "But I said in my abundance, I shall never be moved"; and, "You have tested me with fire, and no iniquity was found in me." The Lord willed that he be subjected to temptation, so that he would not claim for himself anything beyond what is human; for strength is made perfect in weakness. Nor did he act from a bloodthirsty disposition. Nothing could less be ascribed to the holy prophet. Even as he was departing this life, with his last words he charged his son Solomon to remove from him the innocent blood that Joab, the commander of his army, had shed when Abner, although he was commander of the opposing army, fell to a treacherous attack while negotiating an alliance. David wept for Abner, walked behind his bier with the insignia of his power laid aside, and saw to the due rites of his funeral. By this act he taught that a promise made even to enemies must be kept, and that courage must be honored even in an enemy. Did not a man so gentle, by the inheritance of his own devotion, wipe away even the blemish of this error?

And how splendid it was that, when he had given offense by numbering the people and three conditions were offered him to choose from, he chose the third! He was asked whether he wanted famine on the land for three years, or to flee for three months before his enemies as they pursued him, or death in the land for three days. He chose the third because he preferred to entrust himself to the power of the Lord rather than of men, since the Lord would quickly take pity and pardon. So he says: "I am in great distress over these three; but let me rather fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercy is very great, than fall into the hands of men." By this humility, prudence and gentleness he brought it about, to use the words of Scripture, that the Lord repented of his own anger. Indeed it is written that the Lord repented of the evil.

How admirable, too, that he offered himself to the angel who was striking the people, saying, "What has this flock done? Let your hand be upon me and upon my father's house!" By this act he who had been thought unworthy of absolution was at once judged worthy to offer sacrifice. It is no wonder that by offering himself in this way for the people he obtained pardon for his sin, since Moses, by offering himself to the Lord for the people's error, blotted out even the sins of the people.

Did he cover his sins, then, or not? But who would deny it, when this very prophet taught that iniquities are forgiven, that sins are covered and not imputed by the Lord? He himself taught that his sin had been forgiven, as it is written: "I acknowledge my offense, and I did not cover my unrighteousness. I said: I will declare my unrighteousness against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my heart." If he said "I will declare" and merited pardon before he made the declaration, how much more was every sin forgiven him when he did make his declaration about himself, saying, "I acknowledge my iniquity"! Besides, on this very matter the prophet Nathan also answered: "And the Lord has put away your sin."

So he both merited forgiveness of his iniquity and covered and concealed his sins with love, and covered them with good works. Nor was the sin imputed to him, because there was in him no malicious guile, only the slip of error; and further, because it was not a surge of wickedness but the shadow of a mystery. And yet he confessed his offense and acknowledged his iniquity; he saw the washing, he saw and believed. He loved much, so that by the greatness of his love he could cover any error whatever.

But now let him defend himself, for he wrote the fiftieth psalm about that story. He placed after it the stories of his earlier deeds, such as the betrayal by Doeg the Syrian, which is the subject of the title of the fifty-first psalm, and that of the Ziphites, which seems to be contained in the title of Psalm 53. Yet he put this story, which is later, before them. Doeg, and likewise the Ziphites, had betrayed him before the prophet David took up the kingdom, when he was still wandering as an exile through various hiding places in flight from King Saul, whereas he took Bathsheba when he was already reigning.

Why, then, does the order of the psalms not match the order of events? Because he wished not so much to match order to order as to match mystery to events, and so he wished to fit the number of forgiveness to this story. For fifty is the number of forgiveness, as the Lord himself taught us in the gospel, saying: "There were two debtors to a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Since they had nothing to repay with, he forgave them both. Which of them, then, loves him more?" And in the law you find that the jubilee is the name given to the most solemn return of the fiftieth year, in which debts are cancelled, the freedom of the Hebrews is confirmed, and possessions are restored. We joyfully celebrate this number after the Lord's passion, when the debt of all our guilt has been forgiven and the bond cancelled. Free from every bond, we receive the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon us: on the day of Pentecost fasting is suspended, praise is offered to God, and alleluia is sung. Again, when a girl betrothed to no one has suffered intercourse by force, her father receives fifty silver didrachmas, and she herself shall remain in marriage. By this number, then, even vices are turned into grace. Great, therefore, is the psalm that teaches us how penance must be done.

"Have mercy on me, O Lord," he says, "according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity. Wash me abundantly from my unrighteousness, and cleanse me from my offense. For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my offense is ever before me. Against you only have I sinned and done evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in offenses my mother bore me." Which of us, even when confessing an offense, does not think it should be touched on lightly rather than repeated? Who repeats it a second or a third time? See in how many verses so great a prophet sounds out his sin, how not a single verse lacks a confession of his offense. He heaped everything together, crying out his iniquities and his unrighteousness, joining offenses to sins and repeating them often. So he rightly asks for great mercy, and not only great mercy but a multitude of compassions. What sin, then, would such lamentation not wash away? What guilt would such a prayer not cleanse? For one sin he begs a multitude of mercies; we, for many sins, scarcely think his mercy should be entreated even once. Again, we read that with his great power and his exalted arm he freed his people from the land of Egypt when he led them across the Red Sea, in which there was a figure of baptism. If, then, there was great power in the figure of the sacraments, how much more is there great mercy in their reality! Rightly, too, a multitude of mercies is asked for where there is a multitude of sinners.

"Wash me abundantly from my unrighteousness, and cleanse me from my offense." He asks to be washed not so much more often as more fully, so that he may wash away the filth he has contracted. He knew that under the law there were indeed many aids to cleansing, but none that was full and perfect. So with all his intent he hastens to that perfect one in which all righteousness is fulfilled, which is the sacrament of baptism, as the Lord Jesus himself teaches. For when he came to John, the Baptist said, "I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" The Lord answered, "Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." And after Christ was baptized, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him like a dove, and the Father marked out the Son from heaven, all righteousness was fulfilled. That is why the prophet says, "Wash me abundantly from my unrighteousness"; for great filth and stain are removed not by a slight washing but by an abundant one.

But if anyone wishes to take it otherwise, he can frame his understanding like this. The divine word cleanses, and so does our confession: the one when it is heard, the other when it is uttered. Good thought cleanses, honorable action cleanses, and so does the practice of a good way of life. Cleansed by these, each person more easily draws in the splendor of spiritual grace and, as it were, seizes it into himself. Indeed, the precious dye does not shine out at once from a single dipping of the fleece. First the fleece is steeped in a common juice; then its natural appearance is washed out again and again by one dye after another, and it is changed many times by different colors. Only then is the dyeing applied as a fuller bath, so that a truer and more perfect gleam of purple may glow red. Just as a great quantity of murex shellfish goes into dyeing purple, so in the washing of regeneration there is a multitude of heavenly mercies, so that iniquity may be blotted out. So whoever is washed abundantly is cleansed from unrighteousness and from offense. He puts off a kind of habit of sinning ingrained in his pursuits and character, and forgets what it was like. And it is fitting that he is washed from unrighteousness or iniquity, which is the greater, and cleansed from offense, which is the lesser.

That is why he added: "For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my offense is ever before me." It is no small thing for each person to acknowledge his own sin. That is why he also said earlier, "Who will understand his lapses?", that is, who is so great as to understand them? It is like the verse, "Who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?" It does not mean no one at all, but few; for whoever can acknowledge his sin can turn away from it and can choose what to follow. Many boast of their lapses and think praiseworthy what is criminal: one, if he has defiled another man's bed and overcome a chaste woman's affection, or if by some trick he has changed a widow's resolve. Another thinks it a mark of virtue to live by murder, by the ambushes of robbery and by plunder. Some consider cheating and deceiving to be wisdom. None of these can say, "For I acknowledge my iniquity." Only the one who can grieve over what he has done, condemn the wrong he has committed, and be pricked by his own vices can say it. Hence the prophet also says: "What you say in your hearts, be pricked with remorse for it on your beds." Many horses, when they fall, usually throw themselves about, and those whom the fall did not hurt are injured and broken by their thrashing. Others, as the nature of Greek horses is said to be, when they have been thrown in a chariot race or have fallen by chance, do not move at all, and keep a kind of discipline of stillness and patience. If the fall did not harm them, the stillness helps them; at least the injury is not made worse. Are not those who make a show of themselves in their crimes, and think a criminal lapse a mark of virtue, to be judged worse than dumb animals? That is why it is said, as to a dumb beast: "You have sinned; be still."

Hence he fittingly added: and my sin is always against me. For the fool delights in his errors and thinks he gains by hiding old sins under new ones, and so he exults in his crime. The wise man, however, judges that his sin is against him, and he regards the lapses of his faults as standing against him like adversaries, like hostile battle lines. Whatever sounds out, whatever crashes, his own guilt always confronts him; whatever is said or read, he thinks is said about him; whatever he turns his attention to, he thinks that he is being pointed out by a nod or by people's eyes. Whether he feasts, or thinks, or prays and entreats, his own error is always before his eyes; at every moment guilt knocks at his conscience and lets him neither rest nor forget. Like a stern censor he harries himself with constant terror. Everything, then, is against the one who is displeasing to himself: he is his own accuser and his own witness, and there is nowhere to flee, since he himself drives and goads himself. Yet it is the mark of a good mind to feel the wound of sin. Those who have no pain do not feel how bitter a wound is, and that belongs to an incurable sickness; but those who are stung by some pain, just as they do not lack the sense of pain, so they do not lack progress toward health either. Where there is a sense of pain, there is also a sense of life, for feeling belongs to the vigour and function of life. So the one who does not acknowledge his error is insane, raving, out of his mind; but the one who acknowledges it is surely coming back to his senses. He does not reject the remedies that bring health, but restrains himself; he repents of his fault, thinks of it constantly, and by thinking of it condemns himself. And the righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech. He who accuses himself is righteous; he who is righteous is sober and sound. The righteous man does not know how to favour himself, and does not know how to bend the rigour of judgment even in his own case. He shudders at the memory of his own lapse and blushes at the error he has committed; he dreads, fears and shrinks from every remembrance of it. He judges himself severe toward himself, he flees from himself as judge, and does not dare to entrust himself to himself, since he thinks no one is harder on him than the one from whom he cannot hide, whom he cannot deceive, whom he can find no way to flee or avoid — unless he denies himself and takes up the Lord's cross.

Great is the power of a guilty conscience, and great its torments. Eve and Adam were afraid, and when they heard the voice of the Lord walking in paradise they wanted to hide, though no one was hunting them. Cain too was afraid that whoever found him would kill him. Thus he bore his own sentence within himself: that he deserved to be pardoned by no one. Hence he says well: and my sin is always against me, that is: without any respite, the memory and the very image of my error assail me. Consider how it confounds us when we have done something wrong, how it rushes upon our eyes, how it keeps coming back to our memory. Whoever is ashamed of what he has done will not know how to commit afterwards anything like it, that would make him blush in the same way.

Iniquity comes first, and sin follows. Iniquity is the root, and guilt is the fruit of the root. So iniquity seems to refer to the depravity of the mind, sin to the fall of the body. Iniquity is the graver, as the raw material of sins; sin is the lighter. Accordingly, iniquity is forgiven through the washing of baptism, while sin is covered by good deeds and overshadowed by works as if by wings. Hence this same prophet said well earlier: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. For love hides error and covers a multitude of sins. Great love even forgives sins themselves, as it is written of the woman who poured ointment on the Lord: Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.

There are also those who take the first verse as referring to baptism and the second to penance. That is why Peter too, who had already been baptized, is questioned after he appeared to have denied the Lord: Simon son of John, do you love me? He says to him: Certainly, Lord, you know that I love you. And again he is asked: Simon son of John, do you love me? And again he answers: You know that I love you. And a third time he is asked: Simon son of John, do you love me? And he was saddened because he had said to him a third time, Do you love me, and he says to him: Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you. And three times he was told: Feed my sheep; follow me — as one who had covered his sin by exceeding love. Nor is it without reason that, after confessing exceeding love, he is commanded to rule the people, since even when shaken he had not lost the ability to rule himself. We have said this on account of the grace of love, because it covers sin. Indeed, some have said that the question about love was asked three times because the denial had been threefold, so that the profession of love, repeated as many times, might blot out the fall of the threefold denial.

There follows: Against you alone have I sinned. He was, of course, a king, and himself bound by no laws, since kings are free from the bonds of offences; for no laws summon them to punishment, secure as they are under the power of their rule. So he did not sin against any man, since he was answerable to none. But though secure in his rule, he was nevertheless subject to God in devotion and faith; and knowing that he was subject to his law, he could not deny his sin, but confessed it bitterly like a defendant, knowing that he was held by greater bonds because he owed greater things, since more is demanded of the one to whom more has been entrusted. We can also take it this way: Who can judge me, when all are under sin? Indeed, the Lord said of that adulteress: Let whoever is without sin be the first to stone her. And no one stoned her. This, then, is what the prophet says: Against you alone have I sinned, who alone are without sin. One who is himself liable to sin cannot judge another as a sinner. For every man is without excuse who condemns in another what he himself does; for in judging another he condemns himself. Against you, he says, have I sinned and done evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. Against you have I sinned, who called me to the pursuit of virtue, who instructed me in your law. Against you alone have I sinned, from whom alone the hidden thoughts and the secrets of the mind are not concealed.

And done evil in your sight, to whom alone holiness is fitting. We avoid the witness of men, yet in your sight we commit unworthy deeds. We think it an affront for a man to watch our shameful acts; we know that God is the judge of all things, and yet we sin with him as our witness. And yet in this the Lord our God is all the more justified, because our unrighteousness commends God's righteousness and our falsehood celebrates the truth of God; for let God be true, and every man a liar.

That you may be justified in your words. The words of God are full of truth and righteousness, and therefore whatever the Lord has said about human frailty is true: that their heart is inclined to wickedness and leans toward deceit. And because he has declared that there is no man who does not sin — for all have turned aside and become worthless — he therefore prevails when he is judged, since by the fall of all men he has proved whatever he judged concerning our deceitfulness. So if we say that we have done iniquity, we justify God in his words; but if we say that we have not sinned, we make God a liar. But it is impossible for him to lie.

It is plain, then, that we are all under sin. How great a crime, then, for a man to deny that he is a sinner, since, as far as lies in him, he seems to accuse the most high God of lying and to refute him — God who is so restrained and patient that he prevails when he is judged. For the case comes to trial, and God says: My people, what have I done to you, or how have I grieved you, or how have I been a burden to you? For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt and set you free from the house of slavery, and sent before you Moses and Aaron and Miriam. My people, remember what Balak plotted against you. He sets out his benefits one by one before you, so that you may judge, as it were, concerning the things you ought to have kept, and so be all the more guilty for having failed to abide by God's benefits. What have I done to you? he says. He makes himself the defendant and you the judge. Or how have I grieved you? He does not deny the charge of having shown an offended face, if you have been grieved and God was the cause. Or how have I been a burden to you? He admits the wrong of pressing his claims, if he has been thought too burdensome; he adds his benefits, by whose grace he who was thought unwelcome had no need to blush. In this case, too, consider how the Lord offered himself to David himself to be judged, so that he might prevail. For Nathan says: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul, and I gave you all that was your master's, and I gave his wives into your bosom, and I gave you the house of Israel itself; and if that is too little, I will add more for you. Why then have you despised the Lord, to do evil in his sight? Confronted with the recital of these things, when he saw that, though he was the judge, he was the lesser party, he said: I have sinned against the Lord. So he justified the Lord, since he did not dare to deny his sin. We can also take it this way:

whoever confesses his sin justifies the Lord. Indeed, you find in the Gospel that the tax collectors justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John. And John the Baptist performed a baptism of repentance. Whoever repents does not deny his offences. Since, then, David always had his sin against him, he certainly did not deny what he was ashamed of; he did not deny what he acknowledged. And by not denying it he was surely doing penance for the error he had committed, and so by confessing his sin he justified the Lord and was himself justified by the Lord. For the Lord is justified when his righteousness is proclaimed and pardon is asked of him. At the same time he both justifies the one who confesses and is justified in his own words, as it is written: Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.

There follows: For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me. Who does penance with such feeling? He lay stretched on the ground, dissolved in tears; he tasted no food, he renounced bathing. Why should I mention the rest — that he refrained from royal finery and a royal retinue? He added the confession of his iniquity and handed it down to be sung throughout the whole world for all ages. Behold, he says, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me. Turn your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your holy spirit from me. Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation. Before we are born we are stained with contagion, and before we enjoy the light we receive the injury of our very origin. We are conceived in iniquity — he did not specify whether our parents' or our own — and each one's mother bears him in sins. Here too he did not make clear whether the mother gives birth in her own sins or whether there are already some sins belonging to the one being born. But consider whether both should not be understood. Conception is not free of iniquity, since parents are not without lapses either. And if not even an infant one day old is without sin, much less are the days of the mother's conceiving without sin. We are conceived, then, in our parents' sin and born in their offences. But childbirth itself has its own contagions, and nature itself has more than one contagion. Marriage is good, and the union holy; but even so, let those who have wives be as though they had none. The marriage bed itself is undefiled, and no one should deprive the other of it except perhaps for a time, to devote themselves to prayer; yet according to the apostle no one is free for prayer at the time when he is engaged in that bodily union. And for a menstruating woman the cloth is defiled, and in the days of her purification she cannot offer sacrifice; and the days of childbirth of a woman who has given birth, and many other days besides, are kept free from sacrifice until the new mother is cleansed by the lawful rite.

Therefore, of the one in whom the Lord willed that there should be no contagion of such an origin, the Lord says to him: Before I formed you in your mother's womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet to the nations. Who is so great that such great things were conferred on him? Jeremiah? But he was certainly not appointed a prophet to the nations, but to Judaea at that time, though now he is one also among the nations that have believed in the Lord Jesus. Consider, then, whether it is not said to him who, before he was born of the virgin, had long existed and always existed, and was at work even while placed in Mary's womb, and was so holy that he sanctified his prophets. In him alone both the virginal conception and the birth were free from any defilement of mortal origin. For it was fitting that he who was never to have the sin of bodily lapse should experience no natural contagion of generation. Rightly, then, did David tearfully lament in himself the very defilements of nature: that in man the stain begins before life does.

While he is saying this and confessing the filth of sins both personal and shared by all, suddenly the splendour of truth and the brightness of spiritual grace shone upon him. For passing beyond the shadow by the prophetic spirit, he saw the very sacraments of the heavenly mysteries, whose type Moses prefigured in the law. Wounded, then, with the wound of love and seized with longing to search out the truth, he stretched the gaze of his mind toward higher things, and looking forward into the future he saw in Christ the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. He foresaw the sacrament of baptism, and marvelling at the grace he suddenly cried out: For behold, you have loved truth; the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made known to me. Not that the mysteries are uncertain, for they are certain, nor are the secrets and hidden things of wisdom uncertain; rather, they were not manifest. That is what it means: that they had been made manifest to no one. For what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, this God has prepared for those who love him. Seeing these things, then, he says: Behold, no longer in shadow nor in figure, not in a type, but in truth the light shines openly. Behold, now I look upon the truth, I recognize the splendour of truth; now, O Lord our God, I revere you with greater love. For behold, you have loved truth: not through a mirror, not in a riddle, but face to face you have shown yourself to me, O Christ; I find you in your sacraments. These are the true sacraments of your wisdom, by which the hidden places of the mind are cleansed.

And so, now glad and secure because the fullness of wisdom had flashed upon him, he says to the Lord: You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow. He does well both not to make void the sacraments of the Old Testament and to teach that the mysteries of the gospel are to be preferred. He asks to be cleansed with hyssop according to the law; he longs to be washed according to the gospel; and he reckons that if he is washed he will be made whiter than snow. Whoever wished to be cleansed by the figurative baptism was sprinkled with the blood of a lamb by means of a bunch of hyssop. But he is truly washed who is cleansed by the stream of the eternal fountain, and he is made whiter than snow whose guilt is forgiven. Indeed, it is said of the soul itself: Who is this who comes up made white? Before she was baptized, she was the one who said: I am black and beautiful, O daughter of Jerusalem. For she was black, disfigured by the dark horror of sins; but after she was washed by baptism and received the forgiveness of her offences, she went up to Christ made white. So too the Lord spoke through Isaiah, saying: Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow; that is, though they be bloody, though they be foul, I will cleanse them. This is the spiritual snow of which the Gospel says that the garments of the Lord Jesus shone like snow, because his flesh knew no sin — the flesh which he put on when he came into this world, pure from every [?] offence. Why are you surprised that he saw the sacraments of baptism, when earlier, where he described the Lord's passion, he said: The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has set me in a green place, he has brought me up beside the water of refreshment; and elsewhere: The voice of the Lord is upon the waters, the God of majesty? And of this same sacrament he spoke more fully: You have prepared a table before me; you have anointed my head with oil, and your cup that inebriates, how excellent it is!

Rightly, then, exulting in these things, he says: You will give joy and gladness to my hearing; the bones that were humbled will exult. You have proved, Lord Jesus, that your words never pass away; you have proved the truth of what you said in the gospel: Many prophets and righteous men longed to see what you see and to hear what you hear. Behold, David rejoices merely at hearing that there would be forgiveness of sins, and he prophesies that the humbled bones will exult. Just as all the bones of the righteous will say, Lord, who is like you? so the humbled bones will exult — that is, the bones of the righteous man who humbles his soul. Bones, then, means virtues; bones also means certain movements, as it were, of the mind or soul, which are humbled by sins and exult in the gift of heavenly grace. The peoples of the churches are also called bones; hence you find it said in the psalm: My bone is not hidden from you, which you made in secret. He called the church his bone, and the holy assemblies of the devout people, since we are members of the body of Christ, of his flesh and of his bones. This, then, is what he says: that the Lord's church will come to know all the divine works and will receive faith in the resurrection.

There follows: Turn your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities. It is a common form of entreaty to ask those we have wronged to forget the offence done to them. Speaking in human terms, then, the prophet asks God to turn his face from his sins and, as it were, to take on forgetfulness of them. But since God sees all things and nothing escapes him, he cannot forget as we do, from whom the memory of what we have known slips away after a short time. So he does well to ask God to turn away his face — not from him, lest he perish when forsaken, but from his sins, so that his sins may have no power. For those on whom the Lord looks he enlightens, and in the Lord's face are mercy and pardon. That is why this same prophet says: Let my judgment come forth from your face; for from the Lord's face comes pardon, not punishment. We must ask him, then, to look upon us but to turn his face from our sins, so as to blot them out. For what he does not look upon he blots out, and what he has blotted out will be buried in forgetfulness, as the Lord himself says: I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you remember, and let us be judged.

Sin is either forgiven, or blotted out, or covered. It is forgiven through grace, blotted out through the blood of the cross, covered through love. The same applies to iniquity, which is considered a settled disposition of an unjust mind — although John in his epistle said that whoever has committed sin has also committed iniquity, as we find written: Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity. Sin is iniquity, because in sin itself there is iniquity; yet, as it seems to us, sin is the work of iniquity, while iniquity is what produces guilt and offence. It is a greater thing, then, for iniquity itself to be blotted out, for the root and seedbed of sins to be cut out. Let the evil root be removed, so that it may not bear evil fruit; let every inclination to error be abolished; let every kind of iniquity be taken away.

And so, just as the discipline of wisdom, when it enters the soul, removes folly, and knowledge removes ignorance, so perfect virtue blots out iniquity, and the forgiveness of sins blots out every sin. Hence the apostle says splendidly that the Lord Jesus has forgiven us our sins, blotting out the written bond of the decree that stood against us; and he took it, he says, out of the way, nailing it to the cross. With his blood he blotted out the ink of Eve; he blotted out the debt of a guilty inheritance. Faith, then, diminishes sin. And so the Lord, when he forgave sins, would say: Let it be done to you according to your faith.

There follows: Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts. Earlier he asked to be cleansed from his hidden faults; here he asks that a clean heart be created for him, which comes to one who is renewed by the Spirit. For in the new man the heart is clean: the filth of old offences has been blotted out in him, and no image of iniquity remains inscribed there. It is a great gift to have a clean heart. Hence Solomon says finely: Who will boast that he has a chaste heart? And the Lord in the Gospel: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. That is why David too longed to have a clean heart, so as not to be cast away from the Lord's face.

In the one whose heart is clean, the spirit is renewed within his inmost being. For the inward parts are, so to speak, the interior of the body; and so there are also spiritual inward parts of the soul, such as the 'bowels of mercy', and such as the inner parts that bless the Lord, of which he says: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. The inward parts of the soul are the discoveries of the understanding, the pursuits of good thought, perseverance in the virtues, and finally those things which in Greek are called ennoiai.

A right spirit is one that directs well and leads into the right way. This is the Spirit of truth, or else a person's upright conscience, bent by no sins, or the spirit that is in man. We have not passed over what others think; yet it seems to us that, since the passage speaks of mysteries and expresses the grace of the renewal to come, what is being asked for is the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

Then follows: Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. If one of our slaves offends us, we usually turn our face away from him. Many rich men, too, are in the habit of sending their slaves away and banishing them to their small farms, and this is reckoned the heavier punishment. In fact, slaves would usually rather offer themselves to the whip. If this is thought grievous among men, how much more so with the Lord our God! Was it not from this that the murderous resentment broke out (which ought to have been held back, if any sense of piety could have tempered it): that God turned his face away from Cain's gifts but looked with favour on Abel's? So with a silent look he declared the one innocent and the other a sinner. David, then, humbles himself like the lowest of slaves. Like one caught in sin and guilty of an offence, he begs to be flogged rather than cast away from the Lord's face.

Hear how God casts away from his face, when he says: Take him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Whoever is not corrected before his face is placed in darkness. That is why the righteous man, so as not to suffer darkness, says: Your face, O Lord, will I seek. For where the Lord's face is, there is light, as it is written: Make your face shine upon your servant. Indeed, the moment he looked at Peter and saw him, he also gave him light.

It is a great punishment, then, to be cast away from the face of God. Adam was cast out of paradise, and not undeservedly, for he had first hidden himself from the face of God. Cain too went out from the face of God, not only after committing murder but also after he thought he could deceive God, and so denied his crime. The sinner, then, is shut out from the face of God, but the righteous man says: Here I am. Indeed, when David himself saw the people perishing, he offered himself, saying: 'Here I am; I have sinned, and I, the shepherd, have done wrong.' And so the Lord's anger was appeased and pardon was granted.

At the same time he shows that the saints remain while the guilty are cast away. We must therefore guard the grace of the Spirit, so that it is not taken from us because of our sins. For the one in whom the Holy Spirit dwells is not cast away. Instead, keeping the fruit of the Spirit's gift unharmed, he strives always to offer himself to the Lord. So it was with the one who, when the Lord said, Do you also want to go away?, answered: To whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe.

We must also consider that the Spirit is not taken away except by the Lord's will, just as he is not given except by the Lord's will. Yet when he is given, he does not act as if under compulsion. He is distributed according to his own will, as the apostle says in Scripture: All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one as he wills. Since, then, he is not taken away except by the Lord's will, it is clear that the will of the Trinity is one.

Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit. The joy of salvation is restored to that to which it is due: to rational nature. Joy and gladness are a fruit of the Spirit, and the governing spirit is also our firm support. Indeed, the one who is strengthened by the governing spirit is not subject to slavery. He does not know how to serve sin, to drift or to stray, and he does not waver uncertainly in his purpose. Made firm upon the rock, he stands on solid footing.

Whom do we think is called the governing spirit? Many refer the right spirit to the Lord Jesus, who took away the sin of the world and renewed the whole human race by shedding his blood. That is why it was said: And renew a right spirit within my inward parts. The Holy Spirit, of whom he says, And do not take your Holy Spirit from me, they understand as the Spirit of truth, and the governing spirit they take to be God the Father. And how fitting for our conduct are his words: Do not cast me away from your face! In faith he fears that the grace he has received may be taken from him. And so elsewhere he says: My eyes are ever toward the Lord, and later: Behold, as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. Surely this is the spirit that is author and prince, which rules the mind, strengthens the affections, draws them where it will and directs them toward the higher life.

There are also those who have taken it to mean the spirit of a man, which is in him. Of this the apostle says: For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? Whatever can know all things, and is not deceived by a man's secrets, can hold the governing place in a man.

There follows: I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will be turned back to you. The outstanding helmsman is the one who steers a ship along a rocky shore. The good teacher is the one who sharpens duller minds so that they advance in learning. The excellent warrior and admirable commander is the one who fires the more timid with courage for battle and, after surveying the ground, supports them with its natural features, so as to make up for weakness in strength by the advantage of a favourable position. In the same way, the great preacher of the faith is the one who teaches the wicked. Hence he says, and says it well: I will teach the wicked. He did not say, 'I will teach the righteous', for the righteous know the ways of the Lord. He says instead: I will teach the wicked. Indeed, the author of wisdom and teacher of all says: I came not to call the righteous but sinners. And that heavenly physician says: It is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick.

Whether he spoke in the person of the one who called the Gentiles or in his own, he was right to say, I will teach the wicked. Heavenly teaching can change the inmost affections and turn a person's purpose, and divine action can pour zeal for piety into sacrilegious hearts. So those who lived without the law, and who before were turning away, may be turned to the true Lord. And by the example of a king's penitence, those who commit iniquities and bitter crimes may be corrected. Converted in faith and in deed, they may receive the remedy of saving teaching and enter the ways of the Lord, where they will meet no winding paths of error and no byways that lead to a headlong fall. Those men who have run the course of their lives without stumbling are a model of the good life and a pattern of virtue. In the same way, those who have renounced their past crimes or errors of unbelief and amended the course of their later years are set before those who slip, whether in deed or in thought, for them to imitate.

There follows: Deliver me from blood-guilt, O God, God of my salvation. This can also be referred to the death of Uriah. Knowing that he had ordered his killing, David asks pardon for so great an offence. Although as king he was above the laws, he was still answerable to his own conscience. Desiring to free himself from these bonds, he prays for God's help, so that he may be cleansed of every stain of the crime he had committed. And indeed this holy prophet was gentle and meek of heart, and he always gave outstanding signs of his meekness and piety, often pardoning his enemies and thinking it right not to kill them. It is no wonder, then, that he grieves so deeply that the sin of shedding innocent blood had crept up on him. So he asked to be delivered from blood-guilt, that is, from deadly sins. He praised the Lord his God and proclaimed the Lord's righteousness, and so he added: My tongue will exult in your righteousness.

O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. For whoever praises the Lord will be saved from his enemies, as it is written. And he had certainly said earlier, in Psalm 49: But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous decrees? With his own mouth he had said that God forbade the sinner to recount his righteous decrees. So by recounting God's righteousness himself, he surely showed that this offence had by no means been counted against him as sin.

And he added: You will open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. God shuts the sinner's mouth so that he may not speak of God's righteous decrees, and he opens the mouth of the righteous so that he may speak. Whomever he gives open lips, he absolves from the guilt of sin. And the Lord opens the lips of the one who receives the word when he opens his mouth. That is why the apostle also asks to be helped by the people's prayers, so that a door for the word may be opened to him to speak the mystery of Christ. By the tongue we understand the speech of one who exults in God's praises. That other verse is understood in the same way: My tongue is the pen of a scribe who writes swiftly. It means speech poured into the prophet.

But suppose we take it as said in the person of Christ. Consider, then, whether the swiftly writing scribe may not be the Word of God, which runs through the inward parts of the soul, penetrates them and inscribes on them the gifts of nature or of grace. The tongue would then be that holy body born of the Virgin, through which the serpent's venom was emptied of its power and the works of the gospel were accomplished, to be celebrated throughout the world. To destroy sin, he also took on humility. He crushed his heart, and the Lord chose this as a sacrifice rather than the burnt offerings for sins that were customarily offered under the law. Indeed, he said earlier: Burnt offerings for sin you did not require; then I said: Behold, I come. That is: 'Not thinking equality with God something to be grasped, I come taking the form of a servant. I come in the outward form of the humanity I took on, in the reality of the cross, to prove my obedience in the humility of death, so that disobedience may be wiped out.'

Rightly, then, he says here as well: For if you had wished, I would surely have offered sacrifice; you will not delight in burnt offerings. The sacrifice for God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise. As I said above, it certainly fits the mystery that the Lord Jesus himself seems to speak here too in his own person, since earlier he spoke that verse with clear testimony to his own person. For he is the true David, strong of hand, truly humble and meek, the first and the last: first in eternity, last in humility. Through his obedience the guilt of the human race was wiped out and righteousness poured back. He, I say, Jesus, the end of the shadow and of the law, came as the teacher of humility. He came to teach the proud, puffed up in mind and swollen of heart, that they must turn to meekness and simplicity. How then can sin be counted against one who is the type of his mystery, when the mystery itself brings the forgiveness of sins? Unless perhaps David confessed his iniquity and the sin of that offence precisely so that he too might share in the forgiveness of sin and the grace of the mystery.

For what does it mean that a man confessing his sin sings of Zion and Jerusalem, saying: Deal kindly with Zion, O Lord, in your good will, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built? Surely it means that he wants the gathering of the church to be hastened through the calling of the Gentiles. The church would then spread the offspring of its faith throughout the world, as children not of the slave woman but of the free Jerusalem, the one that is in heaven. And it would lay the foundations of the enclosure of its spiritual walls on the firm teaching of the apostles.

The walls of Jerusalem, then, are the ramparts of faith, the fortifications of reasoned argument and the heights of the virtues. The walls of Jerusalem are the gatherings of the churches, founded throughout the world, for the church says: I am a wall, and my breasts are a tower. And the little congregations of the churches are rightly the walls of Jerusalem, since whoever enters the church in good faith and good works becomes a citizen and inhabitant of that city above, which comes down from heaven. These walls are built of living stones.

Seeing, then, the true Jerusalem and Zion, he said: When you have blessed Jerusalem and Zion in your will, then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness. That is the sacrifice of the body of Christ, who said when speaking of his own passion: Open to me the gates of righteousness, and I will enter them and give thanks to the Lord. And in the Gospel he says to John: Let it be so for now; for it is fitting for us in this way to fulfil all righteousness. And later: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake. Christ is righteousness, so he is declaring that Christ's sacrifice will be acceptable to the Father. This, then, is what he also spoke of earlier: Offer the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord. This is the offering of spiritual righteousness and the burnt offering of fervent devotion and of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. He says that it will come when the souls of believers begin to be brought to that spiritual altar of the Lord. These souls renounce pleasures and delights and drag a plough, as it were, through their inward parts, so that they can bring forth the fruits of godly cultivation.

Or it may mean this: when you have blessed the church gathered from the Gentiles, and the spiritual sacrifice of righteousness begins to be offered often, then the holy martyrs too, who offered their bodies to be ploughed for Christ, will be offered like calves on the sacred altars. As we find written in the Apocalypse of John, under the altar were the souls of those who offered their bodies to martyrdom for the name of the Lord Jesus, so that they might win for themselves the grace of Christ. To him be honour, glory and everlasting praise, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, from all ages, now and always, and for ever and ever. Amen.
